Question eight. How do you implement mini-batching for training? Shuffle the row indices once per epoch, slice them in fixed steps, and index features and labels with the same slice. Ten rows in batches of four give four, four and two. The last batch is short, and that's fine. But don't reseed on every call. A generator that seeds itself the same way each time deals every epoch in the same order. Pass one random generator through the whole run, and each epoch gets a new order.

Question nine. How do you shuffle features and labels together correctly? One permutation, applied to both. Shuffle them separately, and every row gets another row's label. On the breast cancer data, logistic regression drops from ninety-six percent to fifty-three percent, worse than always guessing benign, at sixty-three.

Question ten. What is reservoir sampling, and when is it useful? It keeps a uniform sample of k items from a stream of unknown length, in one pass, with memory for k. Keep the first k. After that, item number i replaces a random slot with probability k over i. The follow-up is why that's uniform. Item i gets in with chance k over i. Then each later item, j, knocks it out with chance one over j. Multiply it through, and every item ends at k over n. In a simulation of twenty thousand streams of a thousand log lines, each tenth of the stream supplied ten percent of the sample. The shortcuts fail. The first k lines all come from the start of the day, and keeping each line with probability one percent gives anywhere from five to fifteen, not ten.
